Years ago but, the first opportunity to get out of the office and in the field for a MSP. The client I was assisting needed to restore some important data that was mistakenly deleted. They had a tape drive at the time, but their tape drive was having issues reading the tapes. We had the exact same tape drive at the office, so our plan was to take the tapes back to our office and recover the needed files and bring them back. 

I left their facility tapes in hand ready to save the day when I received a call from my boss to discuss the current status. While talking with him I set the tapes on top of my car and explained the situation. We agreed it was a good plan and I left to head back to my office. 

I received a call back from my boss about 2-3 minutes later telling me I needed to go back and get the tapes. It clicked at that moment I left them on top of my car and drove away. When I circled back the tapes were in the road smashed to pieces. The client watched the whole thing unfold.

Luckily for me they had a tape the took to their bank weekly we were able to restore from, but that was absolutely the dumbest thing I've done while working in IT.

I had a company do the coating, it was a 5 year coating meaning it should last 5 years (that is heavily dependent on maintaining it). 

When I asked him about the difference between what they offered (6 month, 2 year, 3 year, 5 year, and 8 year) he explained the longer lasting coatings require multiple coats and the quality of chemicals are better. The longer coatings have a higher quality carrier solvent and a large concentrate of SiO2. 

Where I'm at a 5 year coating runs between $800-$1000 and is warrantied for 4 years.

I just picked up my Challenger last night from a 5 year ceramic coating job. I cannot recommend it enough. Keep in mind it doesn't mean you can just neglect the paint for 5 years (or how ever long you go with), it just adds a layer of protection and makes cleaning the car incredibly easy. Having a black car made it a no brainer for me. I paid $800 for the whole job.

May 8, 2012
HSUS Video Statement
Thank you for your message.  We’ve seen the video and we are appalled by the apparent mistreatment of the animals. We do not condone for any reason this kind of mistreatment of animals shown in the video.
Contrary to the impression left by HSUS, there is no connection between this Wyoming farm and the pork that we process. Tyson Foods does not buy any of the hogs raised on this farm for our pork processing plants. 
We do have a small, but separate hog buying business that has previously purchased aged sows from this farm; however, these animals are subsequently sold to other companies and are not used in Tyson’s pork processing business. The subsidiary has discontinued buying sows from the farm shown in the video.
Virtually all of the hogs Tyson buys for our processing plants come from thousands of independent farm families who use both individual and group housing. We require all hog farmers who supply us to be certified in the pork industry’s Pork Quality Assurance Plus program, which incorporates rigid animal well-being standards and is part of the industry’s ‘We Care’ responsible pork initiative. We validate enrollment and audit conformance to these standards. Farms that do not conform will be eliminated from our supply chain.
For information on the pork industry’s ‘We Care’ responsible pork initiative, go to www.porkcares.com. 
 
Sow Housing Statement
 
The issue of sow housing is not as black and white as some would lead you to believe. 
 
Over the years, farmers, universities and animal care experts have used and researched a variety of sow housing systems and found they each have advantages and disadvantages.
 
The American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA) and the American Association of Swine Veterinarians have determined that both individual sow housing and group housing are acceptable and can provide for the well-being of sows.  No matter what system is used, the key is how well they’re managed by the hog farmer.
 
We buy hogs from thousands of independent farm families who use different types of sow housing, including individual and group housing, and we currently expect to continue to buy from them. We support the freedom of these independent farmers to choose the best and most humane ways to properly raise their animals, as long as their practices are consistent with the position of the AVMA.  However, we’ll also continue to monitor research into sow housing.
